title: You've been wondering about cloth pads. Here's everything you need to know.
caption:
You've been wondering. We get it. 🌿

Cloth pads are reusable menstrual pads made from soft fabric layers. You wear them just like a disposable — but instead of throwing them away, you wash and reuse them.

→ Absorbent middle layers soak up your flow
→ A waterproof backing protects your underwear
→ Wings with snaps keep everything in place

That's it. No learning curve, no complicated setup.

title: "But aren't cloth pads… unhygienic?" Let's talk about that.
caption:
We hear this one a lot. And honestly? It's a fair question. 🙋

Here's the truth: cloth pads are completely hygienic when you change and wash them properly.

Think about it — your towel, your washcloth, your reusable water bottle. All reusable. All fine when cared for.

The key things:
→ Change every 2–4 hours (same as disposables)
→ Rinse, then wash with your regular laundry
→ Dry fully before storing

Hygiene is about habits, not the material.

title: Thinking of switching? Start here — not with buying a full set.
caption:
Making the switch to cloth pads doesn't have to be all-or-nothing.

The easiest way to start:

1. Keep your disposables as backup (no pressure)
2. Try cloth pads at home on a lighter day
3. See how they feel — comfort, fit, changing routine
4. Add more pads as you figure out what works for you

Most people take 2–3 cycles to feel fully comfortable. That's normal and perfectly fine.

You don't have to go zero-waste overnight. One swap at a time counts. ✨

Start small. Learn your fit. Then build from there.

title: What a typical period week actually looks like with cloth pads
caption:
Wondering what using cloth pads actually looks like in real life? Here's a full period week:

Day 1 (heavy): Overnight pad, changed every 2–3 hours. Rinsed and soaking.
Day 2 (heavy): Regular + heavy pad. Changed at lunch. One load of laundry.
Day 3 (medium): Regular pad. Felt totally normal.
Day 4 (lighter): Light pad. Changed twice. Dried on the rack.
Day 5 (spotting): Liner. Done.
Day 6–7: Everything washed, dried, stored away until next month.

The routine is simpler than it sounds once you've done it once. 💧

title: Why is my cloth pad moving around? Here's how to fix it.
caption:
If your cloth pad is shifting or bunching, it's almost always one of these three things:

1. Your underwear is too loose or slippery
   → Try snug, well-fitting cotton undies

2. The pad shape isn't right for your body
   → Some people need wider, some need longer

3. The snaps aren't sitting flat against the gusset
   → Re-snap and adjust forward or backward

It usually takes a cycle or two to nail your fit. You're not doing it wrong — you're learning.

title: Cotton vs bamboo vs hemp — which fabric is actually better?
caption:
Not all cloth pads are made the same. Here's what the fabrics are actually like:

🌿 Cotton — breathable, familiar, easy to care for. Great starting point.
🎋 Bamboo — often softer, slightly more absorbent. Good for sensitive skin.
🌱 Hemp — highly absorbent, long-lasting, slightly rougher texture.
⚡ Microfiber — fast-absorbing but usually used inside, not against skin.

There's no single 'best'. It depends on your skin, your flow, and your preference.

When in doubt? Start with cotton. It's the most predictable.

title: The questions we get asked the most — answered honestly.
caption:
Let's answer the big three honestly:

❓ Do they smell?
Only if you leave them on too long or don't dry them fully. Changed on time and washed properly? No issue.

❓ Will I leak?
You might at first — that's usually about size and timing, not the pads being bad. Most people sort this in 1–2 cycles.

❓ Is washing them annoying?
For some people, yes. For most, it becomes just another part of laundry. Rinse → wash → dry. That's it.

No fluff. Just what we actually think you should know before you decide. 🤍

title: How to manage cloth pads at school — a practical guide
caption:
School bathrooms. Shared dorms. No washing machine nearby. You can still use cloth pads. Here's how:

🎒 Pack 2 spare pads in your bag
👜 Bring a small zip pouch or wet bag for used pads
🚽 Change and roll the used pad inside out — pouch it, done
🏠 Wash at home or when you have laundry access

The key is having a system before you need it. Once the routine is set, it takes about 2 extra minutes per change.

You don't need total privacy to make this work. Just a little planning.

title: Most beginners buy too few pads. Here's what a realistic starter set looks like.
caption:
Here's the starter set we actually recommend for most people:

→ 2–3 heavy pads (for your heaviest 1–2 days)
→ 3–4 regular pads (for mid-cycle)
→ 1–2 overnight pads
→ 2 liners (for the tail end)

That's roughly 8–10 pads — enough to get through most cycles without doing laundry mid-period.

Once you know what you use most? Add more of that. Skip what you don't need.

Start smart, not big. 🌿

title: How to wash cloth pads (it's easier than you think)
caption:
Here's the full wash routine — no soaking bins, no complicated steps:

1. Rinse the pad in cold water after use (optional but helpful on heavy days)
2. Toss in your regular laundry with normal detergent
3. Air dry or tumble on low (check your care label)
4. Store dry — not folded up wet

That's it. The whole thing.

Things to avoid: bleach, fabric softener, high heat, harsh additives. These can damage the fabric and reduce absorbency over time.

The simpler the routine, the longer they last. 🌿

title: Can cloth pads be used for postpartum bleeding?
caption:
Yes — and many people find them genuinely more comfortable postpartum.

Here's what to consider:

→ You'll need larger and more absorbent pads than usual
→ Overnight pads or heavy pads are usually the right starting point
→ Change them frequently — postpartum flow can be heavy, especially early on
→ Make sure they are fully dry between wears

Soft fabric can also feel gentler than the plastic-backed options that often come in hospital packs.

If you're planning ahead, add a few extra-heavy or overnight pads to your postpartum prep. 🌸

caption:

✅ If parts are still usable (like snaps), consider repurposing them.

The good news: a well-cared-for cloth pad should last for years before you reach this question.

And even when it's done — it's replaced far fewer single-use products than you'd think. 🌿

title: Something not working? Here are the most common cloth pad problems — and how to fix them.
caption:
Most cloth pad problems have simple fixes. Here's a quick reference:

🔧 Shifting / moving: underwear too loose. Try snug cotton undies.
🔧 Leaking at the edges: pad too narrow. Try a wider size.
🔧 Back leaks: pad too short at the rear. Try a longer style.
🔧 Smell after washing: may not have dried fully. Always dry completely before storing.
🔧 Less absorbent over time: detergent build-up. Wash without additives once.
🔧 Snaps coming undone: may be worn. Check and replace if needed.

Save this and use it as a reference when something feels off.

title: Singapore humidity + cloth pads: here's what actually happens
caption:
Let's talk about the thing nobody mentions in the overseas guides: our humidity.

Yes, cloth pads dry slower here than in a dry climate. Here's how to work with it, not against it:

→ Hang pads near a fan or in front of an aircon vent — cuts drying time noticeably
→ Avoid leaving them in the bathroom if it doesn't get airflow
→ A slimmer pad in your rotation dries faster on humid days
→ If it's not bone dry, it's not ready to store

This is the one thing we wish someone told us when we started. Save this for laundry day. 🇸🇬
